headline: Private subnets are now on the public route table, destroying the private/public boundary and likely breaking outbound egress for instances that have no public IP
suppressed: Did not flag the existing NAT gateway or security groups — those are pre-existing and unmodified by this PR.

findings.evidence_ref: network.tf: route_table_id changed from aws_route_table.private.id to aws_route_table.public.id for aws_subnet.private_a
findings.explanation: Any instance in private_a that carries a public or Elastic IP is now directly reachable from the internet; the private subnet boundary that was deliberately separating application/data tier from the internet no longer exists.

findings.evidence_ref: network.tf: route_table_id changed from aws_route_table.private.id to aws_route_table.public.id for aws_subnet.private_b
findings.explanation: Same exposure as private_a — both app subnets lose their isolation simultaneously, maximising blast radius.

findings.evidence_ref: Public route table routes 0.0.0.0/0 via the Internet Gateway; private instances have no public IP
findings.explanation: An Internet Gateway only forwards traffic for instances that own a public IP address; private instances without one will have their outbound traffic silently dropped, so the stated goal of relieving NAT rate-limiting will not be achieved by this change alone.
